title: Simple Machines: Trading Force for Distance
hook: A lever lets a child lift a piano — but there's no free lunch. Simple machines multiply your force only by making you move a longer distance.
key_points: Levers, ramps, pulleys, wheels, screws, and wedges are the classic simple machines.
They give mechanical advantage: a small force does a big job.
You pay for it in extra distance — total work stays the same (minus friction).
They redirect and multiply force; they never create energy out of nothing.
content_html: Simple machines are the basic tools that change how a force acts: levers, ramps (inclined planes), pulleys, wheels and axles, screws, and wedges. Each one gives you mechanical advantage — the ability to do a big job with a small force. A long lever, a gentle ramp, or a block-and-tackle can let one person move loads they could never lift directly.
extra_html: The catch is that you never get something for nothing. Whatever force a machine saves you, it charges back in distance: to lift a load a little with a lever, you push the other end down a lot; to raise a weight gently up a ramp, you push it along a much longer path. The product of force and distance — the work — comes out roughly the same, and friction makes the real output a touch less than your input. Simple machines don't create energy; they just reshape how you deliver it, which is exactly why conservation of energy still holds. Wikipedia catalogs the six classic types and the force-versus-distance trade behind each.

related.title: Work and Power: Energy and How Fast You Spend It
related.hook: Lifting a box and dropping it back does zero net work. Work is force times distance moved along it — and power is how fast you do that work.

related.title: Conservation of Energy
related.hook: Energy is never created or destroyed — it only changes form. That single rule is one of the most powerful ideas in all of physics.

flashcards.back_html: It's how much a simple machine multiplies your input force. The trade-off: you must move the input over a longer distance to gain it.

flashcards.prompt: Why does pushing a heavy load up a ramp feel easier than lifting it straight up?

choices.text: The ramp spreads the same work over a longer distance, so less force is needed
The ramp reduces the total work required
The ramp creates extra energy to help you

flashcards.explanation_html: A ramp is a simple machine: it trades a smaller force for a longer path. The total work to gain that height is unchanged (ignoring friction).

flashcards.prompt: Can a simple machine give you more energy out than you put in?

choices.text: No — it only redirects or multiplies force; energy is conserved
Yes, that's what mechanical advantage means
Yes, if it has enough pulleys

flashcards.explanation_html: Machines never create energy. They trade force for distance, and friction actually makes the output slightly less than the input.
